health-tech-c75c50e27d.headline: STAT+: Ultragenyx drug to treat Angelman syndrome, a rare disease, fails late-stage trial
health-tech-c75c50e27d.fulltext:
The biotech company Ultragenyx said Wednesday that its experimental therapy for Angelman syndrome, a rare disease that causes severe intellectual disabilities and developmental delays, showed no benefit compared to a sham treatment in a large Phase 3 trial.
The drug, GTX-102, had shown powerful results in early trials, raising the hopes of families affected by the devastating condition. Many advocates for patients with other neurological conditions also hoped it could be the first of many medicines that improve cognition, communication, and other aspects of the lives of patients with intellectual disabilities.
The news is a significant blow for Ultragenyx’s business as well. Although the company has multiple approved medicines, they are for mostly ultra-rare diseases, and investors had been banking on the Angelman drug as the company’s path to profitability.

The Voice Test: India’s Next Frontier in Disease Detection, Your Voice Could Diagnose You Before Your Doctor Does
Early diagnosis is one of the most persistent problems facing the healthcare system in India for disorders related to the nervous system, lungs, and psychiatry when specialists are scarce and available only in large urban centres. The magnitude of the problem is evidenced by the findings of a nationally representative survey carried out within India’s Longitudinal Ageing Study, which involved the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Indian Council of Medical Research, and international research organizations, according to which 7.4% of Indians who are over 60 years old suffer from dementia, totaling about 8.8 million people, with higher prevalence of the disorder among people living in rural regions compared to those living in urban areas. Speech characteristics that may serve as indicators of some physiological or neurological processes in the body are called voice biomarkers. This article aims to discuss the measures of voice biomarkers, current peer-reviewed evidence on their application, how Indian studies fit into it, and what limitations exist regarding the use of voice biomarkers for clinical purposes.
What a Voice Biomarker Measures
Voice biomarkers are acoustic and/or linguistic properties of spoken language, including pause lengths, speaking speed, pitch range, or articulation clarity, which have been shown to have a measurable relationship with particular diseases. It is important to distinguish this concept from voice recognition technology or transcription of speech, as the analysis is statistical and diagnostic, much like interpreting laboratory results within reference intervals.

agritech-fc3b4e4c27.headline: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
agritech-fc3b4e4c27.fulltext:
Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

agritech-17a58c01e4.headline: With the monsoon in its final month, nearly half of El Niño-vulnerable districts across 25 states/UTs face deficient rainfall: DTE analysis
agritech-17a58c01e4.fulltext:
Climate Change
With the monsoon in its final month, nearly half of El Niño-vulnerable districts across 25 states/UTs face deficient rainfall: DTE analysis
Of these, 40 are among the 111 identified high-priority districts and most vulnerable to farm distress during this El Niño year
- As the southwest monsoon enters its final month, nearly half of India’s El Niño-vulnerable districts are facing deficient rainfall, with high-priority, low-irrigation regions hit hardest.
- Down To Earth’s analysis shows deepening farm distress, crop losses and emerging drought, while erratic excess rain in some districts underscores a volatile monsoon that threatens food security and rural incomes.
- Around 36 per cent—or more than one in three—of India’s ‘high-priority’ districts, identified as the most vulnerable agricultural districts, have received either deficient or largely deficient rainfall.
- Meanwhile, 57 per cent of ‘medium-priority’ districts and 50 per cent of ‘low-priority’ districts have also received either deficient or largely deficient rainfall.
The Union Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare said on June 23, 2026, that around 315 districts could be affected by a ‘weak’ or ‘uncertain’ monsoon and a possible ‘super’ El Niño. Of these, 147 districts, or about 47 per cent across 25 states/Union Territories (UTs) are currently recording deficient rainfall according to Down To Earth’s analysis of cumulative rainfall between June 1 and August 30, 2026.
The 315 districts have been classified into three categories based on their irrigation coverage. Of these, 111 are ‘high priority’ districts, with less than 25 per cent of their area under irrigation, making them the most vulnerable to a weak monsoon.
Another 76 districts are classified as ‘medium priority’, with irrigation coverage between 25 and 50 per cent.
The remaining 128 districts are ‘low priority’, with more than 50 per cent irrigation coverage or relatively better access to water through dams and other infrastructure.
The analysis shows that 40 of the 147 districts recording deficient or large-deficient rainfall are among the 111 ‘high-priority’ districts. These districts, spread across 18 states and UTs, face a higher risk of farm distress because of their limited irrigation coverage and dependence on rainfall.
When nearly 75 per cent, or three-quarters, of the southwest monsoon season already over and now entering into its final month, around 36 per cent or more than one in three ‘high-priority’ districts or most vulnerable farm districts in India have received either deficient or large-deficient rainfall.
The cumulative rainfall deficit in these districts indicates that the strengthening El Niño pattern might have impacted and led to deficit rains in areas where agriculture is particularly dependent on the monsoon.
Four high-priority districts have entered the ‘large deficient’ rainfall category, meaning they have received 60 per cent or more ‘less rainfall than normal’. The sharpest rainfall deficit has been recorded in Ramanagara district of Karnataka. It received just 19 mm of rain since June 1, against a seasonal normal of 283.5 mm—a shortfall of 93 per cent, the worst among all high-priority districts.
Ramanagara is one of four districts in the ‘large deficient’ category. The other three are in Arunachal Pradesh (two districts) and Meghalaya (one district).
West Garo Hills in Meghalaya received just 412.5 mm against a seasonal normal of 1,488.2 mm—a shortfall of 72 per cent, making it the second-worst affected high-priority district after Ramanagara.
In six states and UTs which include Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Puducherry and Tamil Nadu, all 8 high-priority districts have received below-normal rainfall. Of these 8 high-priority districts, 6 recorded ‘deficient’ rainfall.
Rainfall stress is the most in Assam, where seven of its eight high-priority districts or 88 per cent, recorded deficits ranging from 21 to 54 per cent.
In Manipur, 60 per cent of high-priority districts are rainfall deficient, while in four states—Arunachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Rajasthan and West Bengal, 50 per cent of the high-priority districts had deficient rains.
In Maharashtra too, seven of its 22 high-priority districts have recorded rainfall deficits. While this accounts for 32 per cent of the high-priority districts, the rain deficit is in the range of 28 to 40 per cent.
Deficit rains in the high-priority districts have impacted crops and farmers dependent on them. For instance, 26 per cent less rainfall than normal in the Nilgiris in Tamil Nadu reduced green leaf production in tea plantations and affected vegetable cultivation too due to low soil moisture. Garlic yields have fallen from 4 to 2 tonnes per acre, potato from 8 to 3 tonnes as per media report.
The medium-priority districts, where 25 per cent to 50 per cent of farmland is irrigated, are also facing serious rainfall shortages. Of the 76 districts in this category, 43 or 57 per cent have recorded deficient or large-deficient rainfall. These districts are spread across 13 states and UTs.
Rainfall shortages are spreading across key agricultural belts, with districts such as Hassan in south Karnataka. With 63 per cent below normal rainfall, the district faces a drought-like situation, the farmers are under stress and are unable to grow ragi as per a media report.
Nalbari district in Assam has recorded a massive rainfall deficit of 61 per cent. The staggering 67 per cent monsoon deficit in North Garo Hills of Meghalaya leaves rain-fed agriculture there on the brink of collapse. Rain deficit means reduction in soil moisture that would be a risk to the paddy harvest in the region.
Furthermore, a prolonged dry spell could lower discharge from natural springs, the primary source of drinking water for the rural areas. These shortages could put both food security and farm incomes at risk.
Low-priority status (more than 50 per cent irrigation) is not a shield against severe atmospheric drought. Among the 128 low-priority districts, 64—or half—have recorded deficient or large-deficient rainfall
Irrigation alone cannot make up for a prolonged lack of monsoon rain in these districts, which is also important for recharging groundwater and other water sources.
For instance, Tamil Nadu’s Krishnagiri district categorised as medium priority, received 40 per cent less rainfall than normal, leaving farmers in deep distress, with around 90 per cent of the groundnut crop damaged by drought.
According to the latest assessment by the India Drought Monitor, 39.8 per cent of India’s area is currently under drought. This is an expansion of 1.0 percentage point compared to the previous week’s 38.9 per cent.
The rainfall deficit is leading to drought conditions in several high-, medium- and low-priority districts vulnerable to El Niño. According to the India Drought Monitor, at least nine of the 111 high-priority districts including Kamrup, Kamrup Metropolitan, Tawang, West Kameng, Wardha, Imphal East, Tengnoupal and Kalimpong have reported drought across their entire area
While 147 El Niño-prone districts are facing deficient rainfall, 30 have received excess or large-excess rainfall. Of these, 19 are high-priority districts.
Among the high-priority districts, 36 per cent have received deficient rainfall, while 17 per cent have received excess or large-excess rainfall. This shows how uneven and erratic the monsoon has been across these districts.
These include two districts—Bageshwar and Udhampur with large rainfall surpluses. Bageshwar received around 152 per cent more rainfall than normal, increasing the risk of waterlogging and flooding.
Nashik recorded a 55 per cent rainfall surplus during the monsoon season so far, based on cumulative rainfall between June 1 and August 30, 2026. The India Meteorological Department’s cumulative weekly rainfall data shows a sharp reversal in the district’s rainfall pattern. Nashik experienced deficient to large deficient rainfall for four consecutive weeks, from June 10 to July 1. Since July 8, however, it has recorded excess to large excess rainfall for eight consecutive weeks.
This erratic rainfall has compounded problems for Nashik’s onion farmers. Unseasonal summer rain had already affected the quality and storage life of rabi onions, which are harvested in March-April and stored for sale over the following months. Poor rainfall in the early monsoon then delayed the planting of kharif onions. Heavy rain later in the season brought another risk, with waterlogging and excess moisture threatening standing crops and increasing the chances of damage to onions in storage.
Nashik, India’s largest onion-producing district, shows that agricultural risk is not simply about too little rain. Farmers can face a dry spell when crops need water, followed by intense rainfall that can damage crops and disrupt harvesting, storage and marketing.
The rainfall data points to a highly uneven and increasingly volatile monsoon, with serious implications for India’s rain-dependent agriculture. For India’s most rain-dependent farming districts, the larger challenge is increasingly unpredictable rainfall—too little rain when crops need it, followed by too much rain over short periods.

indian-startups-1d51028393.headline: Simple Energy Launches Wave Family Escooter At ₹1.1 Lakh
indian-startups-1d51028393.fulltext: Bengaluru-based electric two-wheeler startup Simple Energy has launched its first family escooter, the Simple Wave, at an introductory starting price of ₹1.10 Lakh (ex-showroom). The lineup comprises six models across three variants: the Simple Wave S, Simple Wave, and Simple Wave+. All of them have different battery capacities, displays, and connected features. The top-end Simple Wave+ comes with a 5 kWh battery pack, an IDC-certified range of 243 km, and a top speed of 90 kmph. It is powered by a 6.4 kW permanent magnet synchronous motor, which generates 179 Nm of wheel torque. The other models come with battery capacities of 3.7 kWh, 2.7 kWh, and 2.2 kWh, offering IDC-certified ranges of 171 km, 132 km, and 110 km, respectively. Bookings for the Simple Wave have opened across the startup’s stores and website, with deliveries scheduled to begin in the last week of September. The escooter range comes with portable chargers and supports both standard and fast charging. Simple Energy claimed that its top model supports 0-80% charging in a minimum 2 hours and 15 minutes. Simple Energy’s Expansion Simple Energy was founded in 2019 by Rajkumar and Shreshth Mishra, while Ankit Gupta later joined the startup as a cofounder. It competes against Ola Electric, Ather Energy, TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto, and Hero MotorCorp in the electric two-wheeler segment. Simple Energy currently has the capacity to manufacture 3,000 scooters a month. The startup said it is currently selling around 1,500 escooters a month through more than 75 outlets across 63 cities. It plans to increase monthly sales to 10,000 units by March 2027 by expanding its production capacity and retail network. It expects its manufacturing capacity utilisation to rise to 75-80% by the end of the next financial year from around 35% currently. In June, the startup raised ₹250 Cr in a mix of debt and equity as it prepared to transition into a full-stack EV OEM and gear up for an IPO. Simple Energy plans to use the capital primarily to scale up manufacturing capacity and expand production, while the remaining funds will go toward sales, marketing, and R&D to strengthen its product roadmap and customer experience. Its investors include the family office of Thyrocare founder Arokiaswamy Velumani, Haran Family Office, Desai Family Office, and Vasavi Family Office. The startup has raised more than $84 Mn to date. EV Launches Gather Pace The Simple Wave’s launch comes days after rivals Ola Electric and Ather Energy rolled out new scooters targeting the mass-market E2W segment. Last week, Ola Electric launched its S1Z escooter in two variants priced at ₹79,999 and ₹99,999. The variants offer IDC-certified ranges of 179 km and 301 km, respectively. The S1Z is Ola Electric’s first scooter range powered by its locally developed 46-series LFP Bharat Cell technology. Around the same time, Ather Energy launched the Konarc family escooter at a starting price of ₹99,999. The scooter, built on Ather’s new EL platform, comes in six variants across the S and Z product lines and offers IDC-certified range options of 100 km, 120 km, 165 km, and 200 km. The launches come as electric two-wheeler manufacturers increasingly focus on affordable models, practical range, and commuter-oriented designs to attract buyers beyond the premium early-adopter segment. As per Vahan data, electric two-wheeler registrations fell 16.2% MoM to 1.72 Lakh units in August from 2.05 Lakh units in July. However, registrations jumped 64% YoY from 1.05 Lakh units in August last year.

india-deep-tech-36c08bbc9c.headline: AITAN raises $41 million to take Israeli combat drone technology global
india-deep-tech-36c08bbc9c.fulltext:
AITAN raises $41 million to take Israeli combat drone technology global
The company, whose systems have been used by Israeli forces since October 7, has accumulated more than 500,000 operational flight hours. Its new funding will help expand technology developed through combat experience in Israel to the country’s allies.
Drone company AITAN, formerly known as eyesAtop, has raised $41 million in its first significant funding round. The round was co-led by Deep33 and Dell Technologies Capital, with participation from Gokul Rajaram, a board member at Pinterest and Coinbase. Other investors include Benjamin Ling of Bling Capital and Kevin Weil of Scribble Ventures. Including previous funding, AITAN has raised a total of $54 million.
AITAN develops artificial intelligence-based combat systems that have been used by Israeli forces since October 7 in highly challenging combat conditions. Its technology is designed to enable robotic forces to carry out complex combat missions while reducing the exposure of soldiers to risk.
The company was built on the technology of eyesAtop, a small veteran startup founded more than a decade ago by Yinon Atzmon, Idan Yitzhak, Ben Barkay, and Einav Harazi. In 2025, entrepreneurs Udi Oster and Daniel Almog acquired the company’s technology, seeking to capitalize on the surge in demand for drone technologies following the war in Israel. The two serve as AITAN’s joint CEOs, and the company employs about 50 people at its offices in Ramat Gan.
A few months ago, the company changed its name to AITAN in memory of Oster’s younger brother, Eitan, an Egoz officer who was killed in Lebanon in September 2024.
Oster and Almog met while serving together in Unit 8200 and, after leaving the military in 2014, founded the startup Tapingo. The company developed an online food-ordering management platform and was sold to U.S. delivery company Grubhub for $150 million in 2018.
AITAN’s main product is an operating system for drones that allows militaries to deploy and operate robotic combat systems at scale while maintaining operational continuity even when supply chains are disrupted.
The experience of the wars in Israel and Ukraine has highlighted the operational and logistical challenges involved in deploying robotic combat systems on a large scale. Unlike traditional weapons systems, which can be manufactured and stored for years, robotic systems can evolve during a conflict, sometimes from week to week, in response to changing battlefield requirements and disruptions to supply chains.
Militaries must also be able to manufacture the systems in large volumes, operate them in complex combat environments and make different platforms work together as a coordinated force rather than as a collection of separate systems.
“With the outbreak of the Swords of Iron War, it was clear to us that the only goal before us was to help our friends and family win and return safely from captivity and the battlefield. Three years later, with our technology already having a broad operational impact in the field, it is the right time to expand our reach and bring these capabilities to Israel’s allies around the world,” Oster said.
AITAN’s systems are in daily use by the IDF and the Ministry of Defense and have accumulated more than 500,000 operational flight hours across a wide range of robotic combat missions.
The company recently won a joint tender to develop the IDF’s command-and-control platform for the next generation of attack drones, as well as major design contracts for robotic weapons systems.
Many of AITAN’s employees are reservists and veterans of Israel’s defense establishment, bringing significant operational experience to the company. Its close proximity to day-to-day military operations allows the system to be regularly updated based on feedback and lessons from the battlefield.
“Robotic warfare is becoming a central part of the ability of countries to maintain their security independence, and more and more of them understand that they must develop and maintain these capabilities themselves,” said Lior Prosor, general partner at Deep33.
“To this end, control of the entire process is required, from supply and production chains, through software development and force training, to the operation of the systems in the field, their maintenance and their ongoing adaptation to operational needs. Israel and Ukraine are among the few countries in the world that have gained significant operational experience operating robotic systems, along with many flight hours in combat conditions. This experience gives AITAN a unique advantage and allows it to expand its activities and offer its technology and capabilities to Israel’s allies,” he said.
“We believe that Physical AI will be one of the most significant technological areas in the coming decade,” said Yair Snir, managing director at Dell Technologies Capital. “One of the key challenges on the way there is the ability to connect complex autonomous systems and allow them to operate together in a coordinated manner, even in complex terrain conditions.”
AITAN, he said, recognized early that the future of the security industry depends on the ability to connect different systems and smart networks so they can communicate, make decisions and act together. “The technology it has developed has already proven itself in security environments on the ground, and illustrates the growing importance of these capabilities,” Snir said.

india-deep-tech-55bda881c0.headline: Deeptech startup Minimac Systems raises Rs 30 crore from Zerodha's Rainmatter, other investors
india-deep-tech-55bda881c0.fulltext:
Pune-based deeptech startup Minimac Systems has raised Rs 30 crore in a pre-Series A funding round led by Rainmatter, the investment arm of Zerodha. The round also saw participation from other venture capitalinvestors.
Minimac plans to use the fresh capital to strengthen research and development, particularly in miniaturised treatment systems, fleet automation and fluid analytics.
It will also expand its Recycling on Wheels service by setting up regional hubs across key industrial clusters, while investing further in its commercial, digital and operational capabilities.
Founded in 2012, Anshuman Agrawal Harshit Agrawal, Minimac works on extending the usable life of industrial lubricants through monitoring, treatment and recycling technologies, helping businesses reduce their dependence on fresh oil.
“We built Minimac to keep lubricant in service for longer and reduce the need for fresh base oil,” Anshuman Agrawal said.
Treating and recycling oil at industrial sites
Minimac has built its lubricant circularity model around three stages, NanoCircularity, MicroCircularity and MacroCircularity.
NanoCircularity focuses on extending the life of lubricants while they are still being used inside machinery, using in-service reconditioning technologies.
MicroCircularity comes into play once the oil has been drained, with the company reclaiming and repurposing used lubricant.
MacroCircularity is the next step in Minimac’s model. According to Rainmatter, it aims to create a more complete recycling ecosystem through organised collection, reverse logistics and the re-refining of used oil into base oil.
The startup also runs Recycling on Wheels, or RoW, a service that uses mobile treatment units to purify and recycle lubricants directly at industrial facilities.
Rainmatter said Minimac has completed more than 2,000 projects since 2012 and deployed around 2,500 machines. Its systems are designed to handle capacities ranging from 10 litres to as much as 10,000 litres per minute.
It said the new funding will help Minimac improve its recycling technology and take its on-site services to more industrial customers.
“Our capital will help Minimac deepen its recycling technology, expand its doorstep services footprint, and work toward the re-refining capability that completes the circle,” said Abhinav Singh Negi of Rainmatter.
India’s growing lubricant market
According to Rainmatter, India is the world’s third-largest lubricant market, consuming more than five million tonnes of lubricants and greases annually.
The country currently imports more than 60% of its base-oil requirement, resulting in an annual import bill of over $2.7 billion. Lubricant demand in India is also expected to grow by around 4% to 5% annually over the next five years, Rainmatter said.
Rainmatter said Minimac has also set a target of helping avoid 860 gigagrams of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions by 2034.

Deep-tech startup Zenergize raises ₹33.5 cr in pre-Series A funding round
With this fundraise, the company has raised Rs 50.5 crore to date. It had earlier raised Rs 17 crore in a seed funding round
Listen to This Article
Homegrown deep-tech company Zenergize Technologies, which is developing indigenous silicon carbide (SiC)-based power electronics, has raised nearly Rs 33.5 crore in a pre-Series A funding round. The fundraise, comprising equity and venture debt, was led by Giraffe Studios, which increased its existing investment in the company.
 
The funding round brought several strategic investors on board, including Nikhil Sawhney of Triveni Turbine Limited, Varun Agarwal of Ellenbarrie Industrial Gases, Shyam Bagri of Bagrry’s Holdings, and Raoul Bajaj of Trafigura.
 
A few angel investors who participated in the round include Sunil Kalra, Ajith Pai, former chief operating officer of Delhivery, Sandeep Barasia, former chief business officer (CBO) of Delhivery, Nitin Jain, managing director of Neo Group, and Hemant Daga, chief executive officer (CEO) of New Bank.
 
With this fundraise, the company has raised Rs 50.5 crore to date. It had earlier raised Rs 17 crore in a seed funding round.
 
The fresh capital will primarily be deployed towards expanding manufacturing capacity, strengthening engineering, growing its nationwide service network and sales footprint, accelerating research and development, and building operational capabilities to serve large enterprises and original equipment manufacturer (OEM) customers.
Also Read
Zenergize expects the investment will support its ambition of scaling to an annual revenue run rate exceeding Rs 100 crore over the next phase of growth. The company has, so far, reached an annual revenue run rate of Rs 30 crore and built an order book exceeding Rs 150 crore within a year of commercialisation.
The company, founded by IIT and IIM alumni, said it has built the country’s first indigenous SiC-based DC fast charger and solar inverter platforms. With automotive certifications for its chargers and BIS certification for its solar inverters, Zenergize is currently scaling manufacturing and expanding its technology platform.
 
Commenting on the fundraise, Navneet Daga, co-founder and CEO of Zenergize, said, "The past year has demonstrated that world-class power electronics can be designed, manufactured and commercially viable in India. Our next phase is about building the manufacturing scale, engineering capability and customer partnerships required to make Indian technology globally competitive."

india-b0206d4db2.headline: Rubio says no India-Iran trade talks at Modi-Pezeshkian meet, warns nations against evading Iran sanctions
india-b0206d4db2.fulltext:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has warned countries against helping Iran circumvent US sanctions, two days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Bishkek.
Rubio, however, said he did not believe India and Iran were discussing a trade deal. He made the remarks during an interview with Fox News Radio’s The Brian Kilmeade Show on Wednesday, in response to a question about Modi’s meeting with Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit.
“Well, I don’t think there’s a trade deal between India and Iran,” Rubio said, while acknowledging that countries have the right to develop their own foreign policies and that many countries maintain contact with Tehran.
Rubio Warns Of US Sanctions
Rubio said US President Donald Trump had made Washington’s position clear: countries should not help Iran circumvent US sanctions.
“No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon,” Rubio said.
“And if countries decide to do that, then we’re going to have to sanction them too,” he added. Rubio also noted that the US itself had maintained contact with elements of the Iranian regime during previous discussions. However, he said Washington drew a line at activities that could help Tehran generate revenue or bypass US sanctions.
The warning comes as the Trump administration steps up economic pressure on Iran and has threatened sanctions against countries and entities conducting business with Tehran.
What Happened At Modi-Pezeshkian Meet?
Modi met Pezeshkian in Bishkek on Monday for bilateral talks amid the Iran-US conflict.
During the meeting, Modi said India wanted to “expand and diversify” its trade basket with Iran and reiterated New Delhi’s support for efforts aimed at securing lasting peace in West Asia.
The two leaders also discussed the regional conflict, the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, and the need to safeguard freedom of navigation and commerce.
According to the Indian side's readout, Modi also stressed the need to protect commercial shipping and seafarers as fighting in the region continues to disrupt maritime traffic.
India has continued its engagement with Iran over Chabahar port, a key connectivity project involving the two countries. The project has also required New Delhi to navigate US sanctions on Iran.
Pezeshkian Seeks India's Diplomatic Role
Pezeshkian urged Modi to use India’s wide-ranging contacts with countries involved in the conflict to encourage dialogue and help end the fighting, according to an Iranian readout of the meeting.
The Iranian president said Tehran remained committed to its obligations under existing agreements but accused Washington of failing to fulfil its commitments.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran has remained committed to the obligations it has undertaken within the framework of the agreements, but unfortunately, the American side has failed to fulfill its commitments,” Pezeshkian said.
India Balances Ties With US And Iran
India maintains longstanding economic and strategic ties with Iran while simultaneously pursuing a major strategic relationship with the United States.
New Delhi has consistently advocated dialogue and diplomacy to resolve conflicts in West Asia, while seeking to protect its trade, connectivity and broader strategic interests.
Modi’s meeting with Pezeshkian highlights New Delhi’s effort to maintain engagement with Tehran while navigating its strategic relationship with Washington.

india-d5343dae30.headline: India offers flood-ravaged Nepal a hand in rebuilding hydropower, infra
india-d5343dae30.fulltext:
India has offered to help Nepal get its hydropower plants, roads and bridges back on their feet after devastating floods and landslides ravaged critical infrastructure across the Himalayan country, according to three officials aware of the developments. They said state-run hydropower majors NHPC Ltd and SJVN Ltd have offered technical assistance towards the effort, deepening New Delhi’s role in rebuilding infrastructure in the country, where it is already a major energy partner.
Around 700 megMW of hydropower capacity have been knocked out, while key roads and bridges have been washed away by the floods on 26 August. Over 1,100 people have been reported killed by the floods, while over 4,800 people are still missing.
"The Centre and the hydro PSUs have assured that they can provide technical assistance to restore the damaged hydro power projects in Nepal. It would, however, depend upon the Nepalese authorities' decision on the matter," said an official in the know of the development.
Queries emailed to the ministries of power, road transport & highways and external affairs, the hydropower firms, as well as the Embassy of Nepal in New Delhi remained unanswered until press time.
To be sure, Indian companies already have a presence in several large hydropower projects of Nepal, including SJVN’s 900MW Arun-III and 679MW Lower Arun projects, and NHPC’s 1,200MW West Seti and Seti River-6 joint project and 480MW Phukot Karnali project. The GMR Group is also developing the 900MW Upper Karnali project.
India is also a major market for Nepal’s surplus electricity, with cross-border power trade becoming an increasingly important component of bilateral economic ties.
"The ministry of external affairs is in constant touch with the Nepalese government. As collaborative efforts are already on for relief measures, support for infrastructure redevelopment and restoration of power projects has also been assured. The immediate focus is on relief and rescue," said another official in the know.
Hitendra Dev Shakya, former managing director of the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) told Mint that the focus is now on relief and rescue of the affected and displaced people, and in due course studies would be done to get details of the damage to power projects.
“Studies will have to be done to know where sludge has accumulated, or where turbines have been displaced. Only after that will restoration work start,” Shakya said. He identified the 24MW Trishuli and 14.1MW Devighat hydropower plants, both built with Indian assistance, as potential candidates for Indian support.
Power availability itself is not an immediate crisis, he said. Of Nepal’s installed capacity of about 4,300MW, around 3,600MW remains operational, against a peak domestic requirement of roughly 2,600MW.
Sustainable safety
Some experts called for regional cooperation to bring sustainable security in the Himalayan region, which is highly vulnerable to natural disasters due to climate change.
Abhay Kumar Singh, president of the Indian National Hydropower Association, called for a mechanism involving Nepal, India and China to assess risks from developments in upstream areas and formulate long-term safety measures for downstream regions.
India’s experience in responding to infrastructure disasters in its own Himalayan states could also provide a basis for cooperation. “NHPC is well equipped to assist in restoration in such cases with efficiency," said Raj Kumar Chaudhary, former chairman and managing director of NHPC Ltd. "A similar incident had happened in Sikkim in October 2023, which damaged the Teesta-V project of NHPC that the company has partially restored."
“The unfortunate incident (in Nepal) happened after a moraine burst happened at the Nepal-Tibet border and there was probably no adequate information with Nepal, and they could not take the required safety measures in terms of shifting people to safer places or releasing water from the dams to hold this heavier flow of war out of the glacial burst,” Chaudhary said. "However, on the Indian side, due to timely information, water was released from the Gandak and Kosi barrages in a controlled manner to curb major impact here."
Neighbour ties
India’s infrastructure partnership with Nepal extends beyond hydropower to roads and bridges, with New Delhi increasingly combining project development with support for reconstruction after natural disasters. It was also involved in restoration work for infrastructure projects damaged in natural calamities earlier.
In April, the two countries jointly inaugurated a 70-metre high-capacity modular bridge in Nepal. It is one of the 10 similar pre-fabricated bridges provided by the government of India to Nepal, to help in the restoration of connectivity following the devastating rains of October 2025 in eastern and central Nepal, as per a statement by the Indian embassy in Kathmandu.
These 10 bailey bridges, worth more than 73 crore Nepalese rupees (around ₹45.35 crore), along with technical assistance for their installation, are being provided on a grant basis.
Earlier, in the aftermath of Nepal's floods and landslides in September 2024, India had supplied 10 pre-fabricated steel bridges, worth 41 crore Nepalese rupees.
India’s involvement spans the entire infrastructure cycle: from financing and constructing hydropower, roads and bridges, to providing technical expertise and emergency reconstruction support when these assets are damaged.
Roads and bridges are critical in Nepal, where difficult terrain and limited alternative routes mean damage to a single bridge or road stretch can isolate entire communities.
“We are ready to repair and reconstruct damaged roads and bridges in Nepal, but would be guided by directions from the ministry of external affairs to undertake such work," said a senior official from the roads ministry on the condition of anonymity. "The current focus is relief and humanitarian measures, for which Nepal has already accepted Indian assistance.”

world-a14c780892.headline: How the SCO chips away at US power without an alliance system
world-a14c780892.fulltext:
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) was born 25 years ago as a modest mechanism for managing borders between China, Russia and four Central Asian states. At its 
anniversary summit
 in Bishkek this week, it looks more consequential – and harder for the United States to dismiss.
The timing is important. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine remains unresolved, while the war between Iran and the US has turned the Persian Gulf into another theatre of strategic competition, with energy markets again exposed to disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. The SCO now brings together China, Russia, India, Iran, Pakistan, most of the Central Asian republics and Belarus, alongside partners including Turkey and multiple Gulf states.
Its 10 full members represent more than 3.4 billion people and roughly a quarter of global GDP. However, its growing importance is not simply a matter of size.
President Xi Jinping has called for the SCO to assume a larger role in 
technology and security
 and to help create a “universally secure environment”. He has presented it as a model of cooperation without formal alliances, confrontation or targeting third parties, urging members to focus on development, security, people’s well-being and dialogue.
Calling the SCO an anti-American alliance is a mistake. Its members have different interests. India and China remain strategic competitors; India and Pakistan have long-standing tensions; and Central Asian governments want room to manoeuvre between Moscow, Beijing, Ankara, Brussels and Washington. Turkey remains a North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato) member while pursuing a larger Eurasian role.
The SCO has neither Nato’s military command nor the European Union’s supranational institutions. Its significance is more practical: it gives states that do not want their foreign policy 
defined in Washington
 a forum to coordinate, negotiate and hedge.

other-interests-a488e1ad3f.headline: Designing physics experiments with artificial intelligence
other-interests-a488e1ad3f.fulltext:
Abstract
Progress in physics has long been driven by ingenious experiments conceived by human experts. Recently, design methods driven by artificial intelligence (AI) have begun to move beyond tuning a handful of parameters to proposing entirely new experimental layouts. The discovered configurations often challenge established design conventions while matching or even exceeding the performance of human-designed set-ups. We frame experimental design as a search for optima over a vast space of hardware configurations subject to practical constraints and organize this Review around four guiding questions: how can we (1) engineer expressive search spaces; (2) build fast and reliable simulators; (3) translate scientific goals into computable objective functions; and (4) develop AI-based exploration methods that can navigate both discrete and continuous design choices. These questions place AI-driven design on a scale from parameter tuning to de novo discovery, and highlight the trade-offs between computational tractability, experimental feasibility, interpretability and solution reliability. Looking ahead, simulators spanning several physics domains, combined with large suites of experimental objectives, could discover unorthodox experimental concepts that are difficult to arrive at with human intuition alone. Ultimately, AI-designed experiments might thereby open new ways to explore the Universe.

opportunities-800bd27a64.headline: Defence Expo to be held as part of Invest Telangana global summit in December
opportunities-800bd27a64.fulltext:
Telangana Government is making elaborate arrangements for the success of Defence Expo – 2026 to be held as part of the second edition of the investors global summit, Invest Telangana, at Bharat Future City from December 7 to 9.
The government is planning airshow, industrial exhibition and special events pertaining to defence systems in addition to seminars on aerospace, defence and space technologies as part of the expo. Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy has invited Defence Minister Rajnath Singh to the prestigious event being organised by the State government and inaugurate the Defence Expo. The Defence Minister could guide the defence firms, startups and young scientists who are expected to participate in the event.
The Chief Minister, who is in New Delhi on Wednesday (September 2, 2026), called on the Defence Minister and explained about the State government’s preparedness to host the event on par with international standards. He sought the cooperation of the Defence Ministry in the successful conduct of the expo besides granting permission enabling participation of aerobatic teams comprising Suryakiran, Sarang and other defence aircraft in the airshow. Steps would be taken to display the latest technologies deployed in Army, Navy and Air Force.
He wanted the defence firms like HAL, BEL, BDL and others to participate in the expo and showcase their latest technologies. The Defence Ministry should extend its cooperation in conducting meetings with representatives of eminent global defence firms as well as bilateral meetings pertaining to defence officials as part of the expo.
Lands for DRDL and airport
The Chief Minister informed the Defence Minister that the State government had initiated process for acquisition of 750 acres of land required for the proposed airport at Adilabad. Steps would be initiated to acquire another 750 acres for the airport as the Defence Ministry sought a total of 1,500 acres for the project. The Telangana Industrial Infrastructure Corporation had agreed to allot 416.18 acres land for the project proposed by the Defence Research and Development Labs (DRDL). The State Government had decided to lease the land on a nominal rent of ₹1 a year for 30 years and the lease could be extended for two more terms by the Defence Ministry based on the need.

Jaipur Literature Festival to celebrate 20th edition in January 2027
New Delhi, The Jaipur Literature Festival will celebrate its landmark 20th edition from January 14 to 18 next year, marking two decades of literary exchange, cultural dialogue and multilingual storytelling, organisers said on Tuesday.
Supported by the government of Rajasthan, the festival's 20th edition will be held at Hotel Clarks Amer in Jaipur under the theme "20 Years of Ideas. Stories. Conversations".
The festival, which began in 2008, has hosted more than 8,000 writers, speakers and artists and welcomed over five million visitors on-ground, while reaching an estimated audience of more than one billion through digital platforms, broadcast partnerships and media networks, informed the organisers.
Over the past two decades, the festival has brought together conversations spanning literature, history, politics, science, economics, philosophy, arts, gender studies, health, migration and the environment.
Its international footprint has also expanded, with more than 15 editions held across countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Spain, Australia, the Middle East, the Maldives and Ireland.
The literary festival has featured Nobel laureates, Booker Prize winners, heads of state, economists, philosophers, artists and other leading voices from literature, culture and public life.
Its organisers also highlighted the festival's focus on India's linguistic diversity and multilingual storytelling, saying it has amplified voices across Indian and international languages and supported translation and cross-linguistic exchange.
In fact, as part of its 20th anniversary celebrations, the festival's announcement has been released simultaneously across all 22 official languages of India.
"The soul of India lies in her literary heritage and linguistic diversity. It is only appropriate that we celebrate our milestone 20th year with a tribute to her many languages through our 'Bhasha Swarmala' series," Namita Gokhale, award-winning author and co-director of JLF, said in a statement.
Sanjoy K. Roy, managing director of Teamwork Arts and producer of the JLF, said the festival was built on the belief that books and ideas have the power to bring people together.
"What has sustained the festival is the generosity of our writers, the curiosity of our audiences, and a shared commitment to dialogue across languages, cultures and perspectives," Roy said.
Preeta Singh, president of Teamwork Arts, said the festival had grown into a leading literary and cultural platform while remaining rooted in books, ideas and meaningful dialogue.
She said the next chapter would focus on deeper collaborations, reaching new audiences and creating greater cultural impact in India and around the world.
